about.hero.title:
Knowledge Without
Compromise
about.hero.sub: We build IslamicInfo because authentic Islamic knowledge should be free, source-cited, and free of opinion. This is who we are and why we exist.
about.mission.lead: The internet is full of Islamic content. Very little of it tells you where it comes from.
about.mission.body1: We built IslamicInfo because we were frustrated — frustrated by websites that quote hadith without references, by apps that mix authentic and fabricated narrations, by "Islamic" content that is really just opinion dressed as scripture.
about.mission.body2: Every single piece of content on this platform has a source. Every hadith carries its collection, book, and narrator chain grade. Every Qur'anic reference includes the surah and verse. Every dua links to its primary source.
about.mission.body3: This is not a religious authority. We do not issue fatwas. We do not tell you what is halal or haram. We show you the primary sources and let you read for yourself.
about.mission.quote1: "My success is not but through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I return."
about.mission.quote2: "This verse is our north star — a reminder that sincerity of purpose, not scale of output, is what matters."
about.rules.title: Non-Negotiable Rules
about.rules.sub: These are not guidelines — they are hard constraints enforced throughout the platform.
about.rules.r1.title: Every Hadith Must Have a Source
about.rules.r1.desc: Collection name, book number, and hadith number. If we cannot source it, we do not publish it.
about.rules.r2.title: Authenticity Grades Are Shown
about.rules.r2.desc: Ṣaḥīḥ, Ḥasan, Ḍaʿīf — shown prominently, not hidden in fine print.
about.rules.r3.title: No Fatwas. Ever.
about.rules.r3.desc: We do not issue religious rulings. We present authenticated scholarship — you draw conclusions.
about.rules.r4.title: No Ads. No Sponsors.
about.rules.r4.desc: Advertising creates incentive misalignment with authentic knowledge. We reject it categorically.
about.rules.r5.title: No Sectarian Bias
about.rules.r5.desc: We draw from across the major Sunni madhhabs and present multiple scholarly views where they exist.
about.rules.r6.title: Always Free
about.rules.r6.desc: Access to authentic Islamic knowledge should not require a subscription. It never will on this platform.
about.method.title: Our Methodology
about.method.s1.title: Primary Source First
about.method.s1.desc: Every piece of content begins with the primary text — Qur'anic verse, hadith collection, or classical scholarly work. We never begin with a conclusion and find sources afterward.
about.method.s2.title: Cross-Reference Authentication
about.method.s2.desc: Hadith are verified against authenticated collections: Bukhārī, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhī, Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, and corroborated with grading from al-Albānī, Ibn Ḥajar, and al-Nawawī.
about.method.s3.title: Grade Display — Never Hidden
about.method.s3.desc: Authenticity grades (Ṣaḥīḥ, Ḥasan, Ḍaʿīf, Mawḍūʿ) are shown on every hadith card. Weak narrations are published with prominent warnings — not removed, which would hide the knowledge that a narration is weak.
about.method.s4.title: No Editorial Opinion
about.method.s4.desc: We do not add commentary, interpretation, or guidance beyond what classical scholars have established. The text speaks; we present it accurately.
about.scholars.title: Built on Classical Scholarship
about.scholars.sub: Our content is grounded in the authenticated works of the classical hadith masters and jurists.
about.scholars.s1.name: Imam al-Bukhārī
about.scholars.s1.desc: Author of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī — the most authenticated collection of hadith.
about.scholars.s2.name: Imam Muslim
about.scholars.s2.desc: Author of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim — second in authority only to al-Bukhārī.
about.scholars.s3.name: Imam al-Nawawī
about.scholars.s3.desc: Shāfiʿī jurist and compiler of Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn and Arbaʿīn al-Nawawiyyah.
about.scholars.s4.name: Sheikh al-Albānī
about.scholars.s4.desc: Foremost hadith grader of the modern era — Silsilat al-Ṣaḥīḥah and Ḍaʿīfah.
about.sources.title: Trusted Sources
about.sources.sub: Every claim on this platform traces back to one of these authenticated works.

about.faq.title: Frequently Asked
about.faq.a1: IslamicInfo is built by a small team of Muslim developers and researchers who believe that authentic Islamic knowledge should be universally accessible. We are not a religious institution and do not issue scholarly opinions.
about.faq.q2: Do you issue fatwas or religious rulings?
about.faq.a2: No. Never. This is a hard constraint, not a policy. We present authenticated sources from classical scholarship. We do not tell you what is permissible or forbidden. For personal religious guidance, consult a qualified scholar in your community.
about.faq.q3: How do you verify hadith authenticity?
about.faq.a3: We cross-reference against the six major hadith collections (Kutub al-Sittah) and apply grading from recognized authorities including al-Albānī, Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, and al-Nawawī. Grades are shown on every hadith — Ṣaḥīḥ, Ḥasan, Ḍaʿīf, or Mawḍūʿ.
about.faq.q4: Is IslamicInfo free? Will it stay free?
about.faq.a4: Yes and yes. Access to authentic Islamic knowledge is not something we will monetize. The platform has no ads, no premium tiers, and no paywalls. This is a founding commitment — not a promotional promise.
about.faq.q5: Can I suggest content or report an error?
about.faq.a5: Absolutely. If you find an error, a missing source, or a misattributed narration, please contact us. Accuracy is the mission — corrections are welcomed, not resented.

contact.corrections.body: Accuracy is the heart of this platform. If you believe a verse, translation, hadith grading, or citation is incorrect, please include the page URL and the source you are checking against — corrections are reviewed against the original references and fixed promptly.

inheritance.hero.badge: Faraid Calculator · Qur'an 4:11–12, 4:176 · Sahih Bukhari & Muslim
inheritance.hero.title: Islamic Inheritance Calculator
inheritance.hero.sub: Calculate estate shares directly from the Qur'an (An-Nisa 4:11–12, 4:176) and Sahih hadith. Every share cites its exact primary source. No madhab interpretation — these are Qur'anic shares.
inheritance.calc.title: Calculate Inheritance Shares
inheritance.calc.sub: Fill in the estate details and select surviving heirs. Shares are calculated from the Qur'an and Sahih hadith instantly.
inheritance.calc.deceasedNote: Gender affects spouse share calculations (husband vs. wife shares differ per An-Nisa 4:12)
inheritance.calc.heirsNote: Select all heirs who are alive at the time of death. Enter counts where multiple heirs exist.
inheritance.calc.matGrandmother: Maternal Grandmother — الجدة من جهة الأم
inheritance.results.disclaimer: ⚠️ Source Transparency: Shares are calculated directly from the Qur'an (An-Nisa 4:11, 4:12, 4:176) and Sahih hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari 6732, Sahih Muslim 1615). The fixed shares (Fard) are stated explicitly in the Qur'an — they are not scholarly opinion or madhab interpretation. Blocking rules (Ḥijb) are from authenticated Sunnah, not from any school of thought. Madhab differences apply only to rare edge cases not covered by this calculator. IslamicInfo does not issue fatwas or legal rulings. For complex situations — bequests (Waṣiyyah), non-Muslim relatives, missing heirs, or multi-generation chains — consult a qualified scholar or certified Faraid specialist.
inheritance.sources.title: Every Share Has a Source
inheritance.sources.sub: This calculator derives every share from one of three authenticated sources. No school-of-thought interpretation is applied to the Qur'anic shares.
inheritance.sources.tier1Desc:
An-Nisa 4:11 · An-Nisa 4:12 · An-Nisa 4:176

The Qur'an specifies exact fractional shares for each heir category. These are direct divine instruction — not scholarly interpretation.
inheritance.sources.tier2Desc: "Give the fixed shares to those entitled. What remains goes to the nearest male." — Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه)
inheritance.sources.tier3Desc: Parallel narration of the same hadith, confirming the Aṣabah (residue) principle and the blocking rules (Ḥijb). Grade: Sahih — Agreed upon
inheritance.sources.share1Who: Sole daughter; sole full sister; husband when wife has no children
inheritance.sources.share2Who: Husband when children exist; wife when no children
inheritance.sources.share4Who: Mother when no children and fewer than 2 siblings; 2+ maternal half-siblings
inheritance.sources.share5Who: Two or more daughters; two or more full sisters (when no sons)
inheritance.sources.share6Who: Father or mother when children exist; one maternal half-sibling
inheritance.sources.share7Who: Sons; father (when no children); brothers — after all fixed Fard shares are paid
inheritance.faq.title: Frequently Asked
inheritance.faq.a1: The Qur'an dedicates more verses to inheritance than to any other single legal topic. An-Nisa 4:11–12 and 4:176 specify exact fractional shares for each heir category. These are direct divine instruction — not interpretations by scholars or jurists. The word Faraid (الفرائض) means "obligatory shares" — the amounts are fixed by Allah in His Book.
inheritance.faq.q2: Does this calculator cover all heirs?
inheritance.faq.a2: It covers the primary heirs specified in An-Nisa 4:11–12 and 4:176, plus blocking rules (Ḥijb) from Sahih Bukhari 6732 and Muslim 1615. Complex scenarios — multiple grandmothers, great-grandchildren chains, Radd distribution, Waṣiyyah (bequests) — require a qualified scholar, as these involve edge cases not explicitly stated in the Qur'an.
inheritance.faq.a3: After all Qur'anically specified fixed shares (Fard) are distributed, the remainder goes to the nearest male relative (Aṣabah). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the fixed shares to those entitled. What remains goes to the nearest male." (Bukhari 6732, Muslim 1615). This is authenticated Sunnah — not madhab opinion — and is agreed upon by all classical scholars.
inheritance.faq.q4: Why is there no madhab selector?
inheritance.faq.a4: Because the shares this calculator computes are from the Qur'an directly. An-Nisa 4:11 states the shares of children. An-Nisa 4:12 states the shares of spouses. These are not scholarly interpretations — they are Qur'anic text. All four madhabs agree on these shares. Madhab differences apply only to rare edge cases (e.g. the Mushtarakah problem, Radd distribution methods) — none of which are within the scope of this calculator.
inheritance.faq.q5: My situation is complex — what should I do?
inheritance.faq.a5: For situations involving bequests (Waṣiyyah — max 1/3 to non-heirs), non-Muslim relatives, missing heirs, simultaneous deaths, or multiple generations of grandparents — consult a qualified Islamic scholar or a certified Faraid specialist. This calculator handles clear-cut cases directly stated in the Qur'an and authenticated Sunnah.

hub.faq.q1: What are the Five Pillars of Islam?
hub.faq.a1: The Five Pillars of Islam are: (1) Shahada — the declaration of faith ("There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger"); (2) Salah — the five daily prayers; (3) Zakat — obligatory almsgiving (2.5% of qualifying wealth above the nisab threshold); (4) Sawm — fasting throughout the month of Ramadan; and (5) Hajj — pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime for those financially and physically able. These are not merely rituals but form the structural backbone of a Muslim's relationship with Allah.
hub.faq.q2: How many surahs and verses are in the Quran?
hub.faq.a2: The Quran contains 114 surahs (chapters) and 6,236 verses (ayahs) according to the most widely used Medinan counting method. 86 surahs were revealed in Makkah (Makki) and 28 in Madinah (Madani). The shortest surah is Al-Kawthar (3 verses); the longest is Al-Baqarah (286 verses). The Quran is divided into 30 parts (juz') for ease of recitation during Ramadan.
hub.faq.q3: What is the difference between Sunni and Shia Islam?
hub.faq.a3: Both Sunni and Shia Muslims share the same core beliefs: the Quran, the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, the Five Pillars, and the Day of Judgment. The primary historical difference concerns political succession after the Prophet's death. Sunni Muslims recognize Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) as the first legitimate caliph, chosen through consultation (shura). Shia Muslims believe leadership should have passed directly to Ali ibn Abi Talib (رضي الله عنه), the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. Secondary differences exist in some areas of jurisprudence, hadith collections, and certain practices.
hub.faq.a4: Bismillah is short for بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ — "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." It opens 113 of the 114 surahs of the Quran (all except Surah At-Tawbah) and is recommended before beginning any righteous act. The two divine names paired — ar-Rahman (whose mercy encompasses all creation) and ar-Rahim (whose special mercy is for believers in the hereafter) — together establish mercy as the entry point to all of Allah's attributes.
hub.faq.q5: How is Zakat calculated? What is the nisab?
hub.faq.a5: Zakat is 2.5% of qualifying wealth that has been held for one full lunar year (hawl) and exceeds the nisab threshold — the minimum amount. The nisab is the value of either 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver; scholars recommend using whichever better serves the poor, typically the silver standard today. Qualifying wealth includes savings, gold, silver, business inventory, and investment income. Zakat is not owed on one's home, personal vehicle, or work tools.
hub.faq.q6: What are the four schools of Islamic law?
hub.faq.a6: The four main Sunni schools of jurisprudence (madhabs) are: Hanafi (founded by Imam Abu Hanifah, d. 767 CE) — prevalent in South Asia, Turkey, and Central Asia; Maliki (Imam Malik ibn Anas, d. 795 CE) — prevalent in North and West Africa; Shafi'i (Imam al-Shafi'i, d. 820 CE) — prevalent in Southeast Asia, Egypt, and East Africa; and Hanbali (Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, d. 855 CE) — prevalent in the Arabian Peninsula. All four are recognized as valid interpretations within Sunni Islam, differing primarily in methodology and secondary rulings.
hub.faq.q7: Who was Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and when did he live?
hub.faq.a7: Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah in 570 CE and passed away in Madinah in 632 CE. He received the first revelation at age 40 in the Cave of Hira during the month of Ramadan. His mission spanned 23 years — 13 in Makkah and 10 in Madinah after the Hijra (migration). Muslims believe him to be the final prophet and messenger of Allah, completing a line of prophets from Adam through Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa (عليهم السلام). His teachings are preserved in the Quran (revealed to him) and the Hadith (his sayings, actions, and approvals).
hub.faq.a8: This is a topic of genuine scholarly disagreement (ikhtilaf). The majority classical position, held by scholars like Ibn al-Qayyim and many Hanbali and Shafi'i scholars, restricts musical instruments and considers most contemporary music impermissible. A second position, held by scholars including Dr. Yusuf al-Qaradawi and some Maliki scholars, permits music that is free of immoral content, reasoning that the prohibition is specific to instruments used in conjunction with intoxicants and lewdness. A third position permits percussion instruments (duff) for certain occasions. The unani consensus is that lyrics promoting immorality are impermissible regardless of school.

verify.methodology.title: How Verification Works
verify.methodology.sub: A transparent, source-first process rooted in classical hadith sciences — no opinions, no fabrications.
verify.methodology.step1Desc: Your input is tokenised and matched against 61,000+ hadith in the six canonical collections (Kutub al-Sittah), plus Qur'anic text and classical commentaries.
verify.methodology.step2Desc: Each match is cross-referenced with classical scholar verdicts — al-Albānī, Ibn Ḥajar, al-Nawawī — to surface the established grade: Ṣaḥīḥ, Ḥasan, Ḍaʿīf, or Mawḍūʿ.
verify.methodology.step3Desc: We present sources, grades, narration chains, and scholarly context — then stop. We never issue a fatwa, personal ruling, or religious opinion. That role belongs to qualified scholars.
verify.methodology.faq1A: Ḥasan (Good/Sound) is the second-highest hadith grade. It means the chain is slightly weaker than Ṣaḥīḥ but still acceptable as evidence in Islamic law. Most scholars act upon Ḥasan hadith for deriving rulings.
verify.methodology.faq2A: Issuing legal rulings requires deep personal knowledge of the questioner's context, local custom (ʿurf), and current circumstance — none of which we can assess. Our role is to surface authenticated sources and let qualified scholars apply them.
verify.methodology.faq3A: We cross-reference the six canonical collections: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Sunan Abī Dāwūd, Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, Sunan al-Nasāʾī, and Sunan Ibn Mājah — plus Musnad Aḥmad, al-Bayhaqī, and classical tafsir works.
verify.methodology.faq4Q: Can I verify a quote in Arabic?
verify.methodology.faq4A: Yes. Switch the mode button to "Arabic" above the input box and paste the original Arabic text. Our system will attempt to match the exact wording and also search variant transmissions.
verify.methodology.faq5Q: What if a claim is not found?
verify.methodology.faq5A: If a claim cannot be matched to any authenticated source, we report that result clearly — it may be fabricated (mawḍūʿ), apocryphal, or simply unrecorded. Absence of evidence is itself useful information.
